The material taxonomy framework can also be expanded to other materials and includes suggested directions for future research and educational reforms to better prepare students for tackling complex, real-world problems involving material variability.

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Omega$. Let $\theta_0$ be a random variable following a given distribution $\pi$ within $\Omega$. Define $f_Y(y|\pi)$ as the mixing distribution obtained by integrating $f(y|\theta_0)\pi(\theta_0)$. The mixing distribution $\pi(\theta_0)$ can be expressed as an integral over the domain $\mathcal{Y}$: $\pi(\theta_0) = \int_{\mathcal{Y}} \frac{f_y(y_1|\theta_0) \dots f_y(y_k|\theta_0)}{f_Y(y_1,\dots,y_k|\pi)} \mathcal{F}_k(\mathcal{Y}) \dots d\theta_0$. Here, $y_1, \dots, y_k$ are independent and identically distributed according to $f_Y(y|\pi)$, and $\mathcal{F}_k$ denotes the noninformative prior based on the Karamata method of sufficiency sampling. This paper investigates the large sample behavior of Bayesians estimates based on this mixing distribution, specifically focusing on Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators. To illustrate, simulations are presented for the case where $f_y(y|\theta)$ is a Normal distribution parameterized by its mean $\theta$.

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing models. This framework establishes uniform data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols to facilitate model performance comparisons across the 2 largest publicly accessible datasets. Empirical analyses using ablation studies and visualizations of latent knowledge representations have been conducted within PyKT, however the code for these results is also incorporated into PyKT for reuse. All source codes and experimental outcomes are freely available online at https://pykt.github.io/.

Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition.

Ten years ago, at the inaugural PxTP workshop, veriT's proof format debuted,  
which has undergone significant evolution ever since. veriT's proofs have found a  
wide range of applications beyond their initial purpose for solving problems in  
satisfiability modulo theories (SMT). These include enhancing the efficiency of  
SMT solving itself, as well as being utilized in both automated and interactive  
verification processes. The veriT solver generates proofs in a structured format  
tailored to its own internal use, which is both cost-effective and high-performance  
when combining multiple SMT solutions produced through product of resolutions  
techniques (POT). Moreover, the format accommodates the decomposition of  
formulas into smaller, more digestible components, allowing users to examine the  
results of complex SMT analyses in greater detail. This article will walk through  
the history of the proof format developed by the veriT team, as well as showcasing  
its diverse applications and showcasing the latest iteration of it.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals.

Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER).

Graph mining applications rely heavily on node embeddings that preserve structure and proximity. To test the validity of novel node embedding techniques, a limited range of benchmark datasets is typically used. In this study, a new diverse social network dataset, Twitch Gamers, has been created to provide a range of target attributes. The evaluation of the social network and the results of the node classification experiments confirm that Twitch Gamers can effectively assess the performance of novel node embedding algorithms.

Our study proposes that earlier observations of a certain state at around 4320 $\\textrm{MeV}$, seen in the $J/\\psi \\rightarrow \\gamma KKK$ decay, were actually misidentified $\\textrm{B}^*_{s0}(7360)$, a $0^+ $ scalar partner of the known $\\textrm{B}^*_{s0}(5325)$ meson.  To replace this previous evidence, we detect a distinct peak in the $KKK$ invariant mass spectrum, specifically within the $K^+ K^0_S$ final state.  Conversely, if this new finding turns out to be erroneous and the state reported by Bashir et al., located near 4696 $\\textrm{MeV}$, was not an illusion, then it should correspond to a excited version of $\\textrm{B}^*_{s0}(5325)$, namely, a $2D$-wave meson.  In this scenario, we predict a clear peak in the $KK$ invariant mass spectrum, within the $K^+ K^0_S$ tail, of a broader structure observed in the $K^+ K^- K^0_S$ mass spectrum. Recent research suggests combining the Swampland program with dark energy's scarcity could predict the presence of an additional dimension with a negative gravity. We've investigated how this extra dimension affects the size and behavior of higher-dimensional Planck scales, finding that multiple scenarios are possible. Using these findings, we've analyzed the impact on the link between the Planck scales and rereceived the following response:

Presenting a cosmological model satisfying the Swampland criteria for Planck scales, we discover multiple Planck phases can exist, with Planck scales as varied as the size of the observable universe. We apply two distinct approaches - extra-dimensional kaluza-klein gravity and a scenario where Planck slits are infinite - to determine the Planck scales necessary for black holes. We find dark dimension influence on the Hawking radiation is significant, resulting in dark photons with energies spanning the visible spectrum. These dark photons may resolve the "Planck shock" problem by preventing a concentration of radiation at the early universe's center. We estimate the start of these phases, with possible Planck phases beginning as recently as $10^{-32}$ seconds following the Big Bang.

A novel algorithm for precise force control in series elastic actuators is introduced in this paper, centered on a cutting-edge force estimation technique called the transmission force observer. This approach was developed to enhance the inaccurate force readings caused by the nonlinear elastic transmission and sensor measurement errors of the actuators' deformation sensors. The study first critiques conventional SEA force sensing methods, examining their stochastic properties that ultimately enable accurate force control through the proposed transmission force observer. A critical parameter derived from system analysis is key in optimizing the performance of the force-controlled system, guiding the achievement of the optimal outcome. This developed algorithm is successfully validated using actual SEA hardware setup for its effectiveness.

A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. When this experimental setup reaches its limit due to the expansion of the underlying liquid, we can study the raft's failure pattern in detail. Our experiments indicate that the morphological characteristics of raft collapse are heavily influenced by noise, but at larger scales, a rupture mechanism is determined largely by the minimization of energy. Not all broken clusters follow this pattern, as some require an additional input of energy due to surface tension effects. We observe that a specific energy input can lead to multiple rupture patterns coexisting, demonstrating our system's ability to display both random and deterministic behavior simultaneously.

We've analyzed a range of SU(Nc) gauge theories in 3D lattices that incorporate degenerate, multi-component complex scalar fields. These scalar fields are part of the fundamental representation of both the SU(Nc) gauge group and the global U(Nf) symmetry group. We've investigated their interactions within a general quartic potential that is compatible with the global and gauge symmetries. By analyzing minimum-energy configurations and performing Monte Carlo simulations, we've studied the phase diagrams, Higgs phases, and corresponding symmetry-breaking patterns. We've discovered that the shape of the quartic potential significantly influences the theories' overall behavior, with distinct regimes governed by the strength of the coupling in the potential.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable.  Our findings are backed by extensive simulations and actual underwater robot robot learning experiments.

This paper explores the concept of sorting networks composed of comparators with multiple inputs, focusing on those with a fixed number of inputs, denoted as $k$. We've discovered that networks with comparators having a fixed arity $k$ can achieve a constant depth, denoted as $O(1)$, if and only if $\log k$ grows at a rate of $\omega(\log \log n)$. Furthermore, this paper provides an upper bound, denoted as $\le 48\lfloor \log \log n + \log k + 0.33 \rfloor$ for the number of time steps required. We also compare our findings with the known lower bounds, which are at a time steps required $\ge 3.61\lfloor \log n + \log \log n + 1.61 \rfloor$. Notably, for sorting networks that use comparators with a fixed arity $k$ and a depth that grows at a rate of $\Theta(\log \log n)$, our research suggests that $\log k$ should be at a rate of $\Omega(\log \log n)$.

We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star comprising two fluids with anisotropic pressures, leading to the derivation of anisotropic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in covariant form. By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Additionally, three theorems applicable to the single-fluid scenario can be adapted to yield two-fluid solutions from their single-fluid counterparts.

Using recent observations, we create a set of models for a galaxy like the Milky Way. By combining collisionless and gaseous particle simulations, we observe that a bar forms in the center within one billion years, along with spiral arms composed of 2, 3, and 4-armed patterns. These features persist for at least 3 billion years in our simulations. However, we find that a bar won't develop if the galaxy's disk has a radial scale longer than 2.6 kiloparsecs. A compact bulge also prevents bar formation, as predicted. Our findings also indicate that a bar contributes to the maximum rotation curve in a galaxy's central regions due to its shape and orientation.

Galactic mergers significantly shape galaxy evolution, especially those involving massive galaxy combinations that significantly alter galaxy morphology. This study focuses on how magnetic fields affect major mergers involving abundant gas, using high-resolution simulations to examine the impact. Conducting this analysis within a realistic cosmic framework, this study employs advanced simulations to compare magnetic field effects on merging galaxies with and without magnetic field influence. Unlike previous non-realistic simulations, this study discovers that incorporating magnetic fields in simulations of massive galaxy mergers has a notable impact on how these galaxy combinations solidify. Although magnetic fields do not greatly alter general features, they have a notable effect on structural characteristics, forming extended discs and spiral patterns in simulations, whereas simulations without magnetic fields yield more compact, ring-like shapes. A separate investigation on resolution demonstrates that global features converge across various levels of resolution and physical modeling but reveals distinct differences in galaxy morphology at sufficient resolution, attributed to enhanced amplification of magnetic fields in high-resolution simulations.

Our solution to the 2nd COVID-19 Severity Detection Competition has been successfully presented, where our goal was to classify chest CT images into Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Critical COVID-19 grades. To achieve this, we proposed a cutting-edge infection-aware 3D classification network called the Contrastive Mixup Classification network. This innovative approach involved initially training two segmentation networks to identify lung regions and inner lesions. These lesion masks were used in conjunction with the original CT scans to generate additional useful information. To rectify data imbalance, we incorporated weighted cross-entropy loss into our improved Contrastive Mixup Classification network. Consequently, our approach earned top honors with a Macro F1 Score of 51.76%, outperforming the baseline by a substantial 11.46%.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a significant margin and best existing domain adaptation methods for GEC in the same domain setting.

The impact of rounding on estimating discrete variables has long been acknowledged but relatively understudied. This phenomenon's implications were examined with a simple yet significant example. Consider a non-negative integer-valued variable, where rounding its average value and applying a transformation (dividing by two) can result in vastly different estimates for the variable's maximum value. These estimates can either be reliable or result in extreme overestimates even with large sample sizes. This research brings together existing studies on rounding effects, highlighting the need for further investigation despite rounding's popularity in past studies.

Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal $\text{GdInO}_3$ through an in-situ gas source MBE process. Analysis using XRD $\theta$-$2\theta$ and $\phi$ scans confirmed the material's orthorhombic structure. Temperature-dependent electrical measurements revealed two transitions to antiferromagnetic phases at $T_N1 = 13.5\,\text{K}$ and $T_N2 = 2.5\,\text{K}$. The first transition corresponds to the ordering of Gd$^{3+}$ ions, while the second transition at $2.5\,\text{K}$ is attributed to In$^{3+}$ ions. This additional transition was not previously documented in $\text{GdInO}_3$ or related $\text{RInO}_3$ compounds. The $2.5\,\text{K}$ transition can be abolished by a 5 T magnetic field applied parallel to the $c$-axis. Furthermore, magnetization measurements in the $4.2\,\text{K}$ range and perpendicular to this axis show that the $2.5\,\text{K}$ anomaly is modulated by the magnetic field.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods among agents, where each agent's valuation function is additive, is explored in this research. We focus on achieving fair allocations under additive valuation functions. A specific fairness criterion, known as "envy-freeness up to one good" or EF1, is analyzed in detail within this research. Under the assumption of additive valuation functions, we demonstrate that EF1 allocations can be found in polynomial time, even when the number of items and fairness requirements are not fixed parameters. Moreover, for additively motivated agents, we show that EF1 allocations can be determined in linear time with respect to the total number of goods and agents, again with EF1 being a non-fixed parameter.

In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of employing a direct one-to-one mapping between source and target domains through translation. Instead, we utilize stochastic translation to account for domain ambiguity and analyze its potential to enhance the performance of UDA. We evaluate our hypothesis of the stochastic translation benefit by generating various levels of stochasticity using noise injection techniques and demonstrating improved results with source label superfection as another method of inducing variability. Additionally, we establish that our HAD approach outperforms strong baselines, including variational adversarial domain adaptation and simple source projection, on the CUAD and MAD datasets, showcasing the advantages of incorporating stochastic translation in UDA.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, stands out due to its unusual, unshaped star formation activity occurring far from its center. Recent research has focused on understanding the environment and internal elements of similarly shaped star-forming regions within UV images, aiming to uncover the cause behind this unusual star formation. Although previous research found no remarkable local interactions with neighboring galaxies, nor any significant gravitational influences from nearby objects, this study has discovered several previously unknown features of UGC 8839 that may be shaping its low-velocity, unstarred morphology. By studying its deep optical and infrared images, astronomers have uncovered extreme star formation activity within UGC 8839, along with notable, star-born HII regions located at a considerable distance from its center. Although the exact star mass remains unclear, by comparing its VCSB color with other star-forming areas, researchers have discovered evidence of high gas content within UGC 8839, along with notable spiral arms and a possible central bar. These star-forming regions provide new insights into how the internal elements of deeply shaped spiral galaxies focus on morphological features, like spiral arms or central bars, may influence the formation of star clusters occurring far from the galaxy's center.

Researchers propose using paleo-detectors, an experimental technique, to detect dark matter. Unlike conventional detectors, which require massive and expensive set-ups, paleo-detectors utilize naturally occurring rocks with deep geological history that contain tiny damage tracks from dark matter interactions. Thanks to advancements in microscopy and the ability to study samples over billions of years, paleo-detectors can potentially offer more sensitive detection at significantly lower costs. This could significantly expand the range of sensitivity in dark matter research. Using updated analytical methods, scientists have simulated the capabilities of paleo-detectors under various conditions and found them robust against inaccuracies in age measurements and the composition of samples. Even with relatively high concentrations of radioactive contaminants, the sensitivity of paleo-detectors can surpass current limits, offering the possibility to detect dark matter interactions below existing detection thresholds, even when masses are less than ten GeV.

This paper introduces a novel form of leakage in modern encrypted databases, specifically 'update pattern leakage'. A formalized definition and security framework for DP-Sync are presented, leveraging differential privacy through 'DP update patterns'. A proposed framework, DP-Sync, builds upon existing database schemes by incorporating differential privacy-protected update patterns, ensuring the entire update history of outsourced data remains confidential.

The extensive use of Machine Learning (ML) in high-security sectors necessitates a transparent understanding of its methodology. Nonetheless, research into decoding ML models like Random Forest is in its nascent stages. To bridge this knowledge gap, we employ information theory to formulate a novel metric for measurement, and apply it to several Random Forest models to fill existing data deficiencies. Our approach yields interpretable results for Random Forest predictions in the form of input-based rule sets. These findings have practical implications, offering explicit input recommendations to achieve desired model outputs. Moreover, our example applications demonstrate the potential for real-world problem solutions such as optimizing costs in classification tasks and maximizing classification accuracy within constrained input sets.

Minimally invasive surgery has emerged as a highly effective treatment, allowing for non-invasive exploration of abdominal organs. Advances in medical technology, particularly high-definition cameras and sophisticated software, have enhanced its efficacy and paved the way for computer-assisted procedures. Although the process still faces technical challenges, we have investigated several popular deep learning approaches to improve automated detection and tracking of surgical instruments during laparoscopic surgery. The evaluation of our methods revealed that a novel deep learning network outperformed existing alternatives, yielding impressive accuracy and real-time processing capabilities. The exceptional performance of the model, characterized by high Dice coefficients and fast frame rates, signifies significant potential for its application in medical tool tracking.

Current public datasets for re-identifying individuals are limited due to the difficulties associated with labeling them. Despite the abundance of unlabeled surveillance footage that can be easily obtained, it's unclear how to effectively utilize this content to develop useful re-identification representations. Typically, existing methods focus on surface-level techniques to label videos, without considering the large computational resources they would require. Building on these challenges, we present a groundbreaking approach by introducing massive unlabeled surveillance video datasets and a self-supervised method to create sample videos for training. By employing this framework, we were able to label over 100,000 images from 8,000 seconds of video in an entirely automated manner. Additionally, our results show that utilizing these unlabeled data significantly enhances re-identification performance when fine-tuned with them.

This paper presents an original model that uses a unique threshold measurement formula in the Realized-GARCH model. The new framework utilizes a non-linear model that takes into account the 'leverage effect' and models the connection between realized volatility and hidden volatility. A specific estimation method was adopted, a simulation test was performed to evaluate its effectiveness. Furthermore, the paper conducts a practical study using real-world data, predicting Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall for various stock market indices with varying forecasting lengths. Results demonstrate the capability of the new framework to achieve competitive accuracy compared to established GARCH and Realized-GARCH type models.

Recent findings from global pulsar timing arrays suggest a nano-Hertz gravitational wave background signal remains elusive in current data. Nevertheless, enhanced datasets are expected to yield statistically significant evidence in the future. This study endeavors to eliminate sampling bias in data analysis. By examining various configurations of nested samplers and traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, we aim to identify the time efficiency and consistency of these sampling techniques on pulsar timing array data. Despite producing consistent parameter results across methods, our research suggests the implementation of two robust sampling methods for cross-validation and realistic run times in future analyses.

Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion is conducted, yielding clear signals for nearly all significant combinations of quark field contractions except one. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory.

Evaluating protoplanetary disk evolution is closely tied to understanding how
mass accretion rates are influenced by a star and its disk properties.
Specifically, factors like disk scale height, viscosity, and midplane
temperature play a crucial role. This work aims to assess these same elements
by observing the continuum emission from infalling material, which is
constrained by mass accretion. A simple model of converging flow is presented
and used to derive formulas that calculate the disk scale height, midplane
temperature, and opacity in terms of mass accretion rate and radii at both
large and small radii. Assuming that dust opacity behaves in a consistent
manner, we can determine midplane temperature from the midplane opacity.
These calculations are then applied to three types of systems: Bepler, Henage-63,
and Henage-64, which are observed to show H-alpha and infrared emissions. By
estimating mass accretion rates (>0.1 solar masses per year), we can infer
properties of these systems. It is found that Bepler and Henage-64 systems,
which have high mass accretion rates, likely have midplane temperatures
exceeding 300 Kelvin at large radii, which may indicate the potential for
molecular water line emission. Additionally, if dust is concentrated in
Bepler, it may also have solar abundance of iron in its disk

This study explores how beliefs about luck influence people's views on redistribution in modern society. It hypothesizes that if people perceive income disparities primarily as a result of luck rather than effort, they will have stronger support for redistributive policies. However, survey data reveals that those who value the fairness of outcomes are actually less likely to back redistribution, which contradicts initial expectations. Ultimately, researchers identify a key role for misguided perceptions of luck in shaping high levels of desired but uneconomically realized redistribution.

Removing a subspace from a partial flag results in another partial flag consisting of fewer components. This action induces a mapping $\pi : X \to X'$ between corresponding flag varieties, which essentially discards information and makes $\pi$ a projection that is not injective. A key feature of $\pi$ is that it maps certain stable maps $\Sigma_\lambda \subset X$ of a specific degree to Schubert varieties $\Sigma_{\bar{\lambda}} \subset X'$ of a corresponding degree. Our analysis focuses on degree stable maps $\Sigma_\lambda \subset X$ whose parameters describe the relationships between incoming and outgoing flag components. For Schubert varieties $\Sigma_\lambda \subset X$ with "compatible" parameters, we show in this thesis that there exists a rational map from $\Sigma_\lambda$ to $\Sigma_\epsilon \subset X'$, which essentially acts as a reduction map from corresponding rational parabolic groups $P_\lambda \to P_\epsilon$. Our main objective in this thesis is to establish that rational maps from degree stable maps $\Sigma_\lambda \subset X$ to their images under the forgetful map $\pi$ can be constructed for an arbitrary arrangement of flag components.

The development of modern machine learning applications is dependent on training data, yet training models to perform a specific task can be computationally expensive. Consequently, pinpointing the contributions of individual datasets to a trained model is crucial, particularly when models face privacy concerns and funding limitations from specific datasets. Unfortunately, existing methods for computing feature importance, such as Shapley values, become impractical for this task due to their computational demands. We introduce an efficient approach for computing exact combinatorial Shapley values, specifically tailored to linear classifiers and dataset removal games, where the value of a subset of players is determined by the performance difference between a model trained on that subset and the same subset minus a particular datapoint. We present two efficient algorithms, including a dynamic programming method with an improved time complexity of $O(n^2+d)$, outperforming the current state of the art.

We investigated the relationship between radio sources found within 22 of the most massive and 17 of the least massive globular clusters in the Milky Way's halo, along with the encounter rates these clusters experience. The study found a significant correlation between radio source counts and stellar encounter rates, with sources likely being induced by planetary nebulae. However, the relationship between radio source counts and cluster mass did not meet statistical significance. Encounters with massive objects induced more radio sources than collisions with field stars of the same total mass. The induced radio source rate was observed to decrease over time in all the most massive clusters studied. We used a previously established model of electric currents in clusters to explain the data and found a correlation between the induced radio source rates and the ultraviolet continuum flux in the visible spectrum among the most massive clusters. These findings provide evidence that planetary nebulae are responsible for the nebular activity observed in many of the Milky Way's globular clusters.

We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two key components: first, a sampling strategy that extracts informative interactions from the projected graph by rating their relevance; second, a formulation of the task as an optimization problem where the sampling strategy is automatically learned. This approach outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques and has practical applications beyond hypergraph reconstruction, including community detection, link prediction, and node classification.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures.

The scattering of coherent light from heated alkali metals in a range of 350-450 Kelvin is examined in detail, and atomic spacings are measured in terms of wavelength from approximately 0.7 lambda to 0.1 lambda. A comprehensive theoretical framework models thermal alkali metals as groups of interacting radiating dipoles, and demonstrates that photon correlation data can be accurately predicted through random atomic pair positioning. Experiments with sodium vapor confirm our findings, revealing that light intensity patterns and related correlation data match our theoretical calculations.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Share-Agents, which aims to transfer high-quality experience to less effective agents. We introduce two key innovations: joint state representations that focus on relevant states for each agent, and a shared value network that captures the potential value of the current state. We evaluated Share-Agents using public datasets and demonstrated its superiority over baseline algorithms in terms of efficiency.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images from the RADIANCE research collection. Our method demonstrated significant improvements in accuracy, surpassing conventional 2D and 3D registration techniques by nearly 5 mm, and a common 4 mm clinical threshold.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay Conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen paper, Einstein believed he had used the instantaneous non-local effect in his argument to demonstrate the theory's inherent limitations. We present numerical solutions to the relativistic Dirac equation when two electrons experience the instantaneous non-local impact of one being measured following the release from their bound state. Our results show that, contrary to quantum mechanics' predictions of merely probabilistic knowledge about individual measurements, there are instances where the exact outcome of detecting a particle can be determined with certainty upon detecting its partner. This implies that the uncertainty associated with each individual measurement is not solely due to inherent quantum fluctuations, but could also be influenced by the instantaneous non-local effect. Consequently, using the Einstein argument, the quantum state may not provide a comprehensive description of reality.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel BC-Enabled FL solutions to address various IoVs data privacy challenges and scenarios.

V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2013, shows a significant optical light curve decline of about 1.5 magnitudes every 100 days for up to three years post-eruption. The V392 Persei system has been observed with the APEX telescope at various time intervals since 2014 using the SCUBA-2 at 850 $\mu$m and with the NOEMA telescope at 43 GHz, both of which have yet to detect infrared or microwave emission. The absence of such emission can be explained by the mass of the ejecta being less than $10^{-4} M_{\odot}$, which is consistent with V392 Persei's previously established low ejecta mass.

In quantum computing, generating the entanglement of any number of qubits in a single operation has significant implications for scaling operations, especially in conjunction with error correction techniques like the surface code. By analyzing the fault tolerance requirements, we compare our findings to existing approaches, specifically consecutive two-qubit gate applications, to reveal the potential advantages and challenges of utilizing multi-qubit gates for reliable and scalable quantum computation.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission.

A type of genuine two-dimensional crosscurrent that flows counter to heat flow has been identified within a generic three-dimensional lattice model. The stability of these currents is attributed to a mechanism of robust counterflow that relies on a symmetry-protected nonabelian knot structure in the system's vacuum state. The research demonstrates that certain abstract knot configurations can give rise to the desired symmetry protection, enabling the currents to remain impurity-resistant. The study also analyzes realistic abelian knot designs capable of producing two-dimensional crosscurrents in three-dimensional space, specifically on the honeycomb lattice. The preparation of these knot states through adiabatic evolution from a trivial vacuum state during a cyclic process is both theoretically and experimentally feasible. The preparation protocol is detailed on the honeycomb lattice, with possible experimental implementations utilizing cold atoms or photonic clusters. The document also highlights the production of nontrivial knot states as an essential final stage in the development of topological quantum computation using scions.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into Dyson's maximum luminosity theorem. In contrast, the conditions under which scalar gravitational waves in Brans-Dicke theory allow light to escape infinity without being overpowered by rapid mass loss.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytic model that accounts for the formation of Population III stars, early black hole binaries, and stellar dynamics in nuclear star clusters. These components are integrated into our cosmological ray-tracing model to generate the first observations of high-redshift gravitational waves from LISA. Our findings reveal that within the future LISA detection horizon, approximately 15% of merging BBH in the universe reside within nuclear star clusters. Furthermore, we predict that one-third of BBH within Population III binary systems located in nuclear star clusters will merge below a redshift of 0. Our analysis further explores the potential for identifying distinct gravitational wave signatures of BBH within nuclear star clusters.

The primary objective of the Gravitational wave and high-energy EM Counterpart All-sky Monitor (GECAM) is to detect various Gamma-Ray Burst (GRB) sources, including merging neutron stars, black holes, active galactic nuclei, and magnetars. By accurately tracking the sky position of Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRBs), the GECAM collaboration aims to pinpoint gravitational wave sources, active galactic nuclei, and merging black holes or neutron stars. In response, this paper presents the response models of the GECAM detector, addressing the relationship between the triggered energy thresholds and the field of view for both single and coincident GECAM buckets. Additionally, it provides parametric functions to describe the GRB simulator response to burst profiles across the GECAM detector.

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and serves as the M\"{o}bius invariant subspaces of the Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1}. Our focus lies in analyzing the maximal subspace of strong continuity for semigroups of operators, exploring sufficient and necessary conditions on the infinitesimal generator of phi for the semigroup [phi_t, BMOA_p] to equal VMOA_p. We also establish the connection between the maximal subspace of strong continuity and the Volterra-type operators T_g, specifically examining which symbols g make T_g bounded or compact from BMOA to BMOA_1, while also investigating the relationship between compactness and weak compactness of T_g on BMOA_p when 1 < p < 2.

Humanity has continually sought knowledge, a pursuit amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, despite employing metrics such as citation counts and impact factors, it remains unclear how a discipline's knowledge amount correlates with productivity, specifically how the value of new knowledge varies with each new advancement. To address this question, researchers compiled 185 million articles spanning 19 disciplines and analyzed the citation networks between authors, essentially mapping the evolution of scientific knowledge within each area. Using both structured and unstructured entropies to analyze the resulting data, they devised the Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI), which measures knowledge amount as a disorder difference created by increasing order within the scientific literature. Subsequently, they discovered that the growth of new literature accelerates the growth of new knowledge, but there is an evident slowdown before this threshold.

In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we investigate two performance indicators for two typical scenarios: first, where the potential eavesdropper is unknown, and second, where the eavesdropper's location is known. Our analytical approach involves deriving accurate mathematical expressions to assess end-to-end data confidentiality and end-to-end data security in real-time. Furthermore, we propose an optimization strategy to enhance end-to-end data security by managing power allocation between two communication links. Our theoretical findings are validated through simulation experiments that demonstrate the effectiveness of our optimization strategy in enhancing end-to-end data security across multiple narrowband OFDM channels.

Two-dimensional systems with robust edge currents due to large Chern numbers offer a wealth of chiral modes related to their topological invariants. In photonic configurations, these edge currents translate to stable multi-mode waveguides that naturally protect the topological properties of the system. In our research, we combine these photonic setups with quantum sources, using a Harper-Hofstadter model to illustrate scenarios where quantum emitters display quantized emission rates. These increased emission rates can lead to significant heating of the edge modes, altering the system's overall thermodynamic behavior.

In the complex context of an urban intersection with automated and human-driven vehicles, we explore an essential challenge: generating safe pathways for automated vehicles. Our research focuses on preventing rear-end collisions when a connected vehicle's human-driven leader approaches the yellow and red phases of the traffic light. We've developed a predictive control system that can instantly forecast how the preceding human driver operates and utilize this prediction to create a safety-oriented pathway in a limited timeframe. The performance of this framework has been tested using a simulation and we assess its reliability.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research overcomes this barrier by significantly enhancing their computational performance, resulting in a substantial increase in speed of up to 2 orders of magnitude across all seven games tested.
Our modifications primarily involve utilizing contemporary technology for virtual reality, implementing a versatile codebase to streamline the virtualization process, and applying highly efficient data structures to accelerate core game functions.
The outcomes of our experiments demonstrate that our advancements are particularly beneficial for virtual agents involved in natural language understanding, they also provide a much-needed boost to the text-based game industry by showcasing the potential for these games to keep up with the current pace of virtual agent progress (around 0.04 points per year).
We believe that combining improved computational performance with cutting-edge text analysis technology can propel the performance of virtual agents in the Inferno game from its present level of roughly 0.75 intelligence per second to potentially surpassing human capabilities in the future.
We have made our enhanced codebase and versions of the ten most commonly used text-based games available for download at https://textadventures.org.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size and memory requirements. Researchers are continuously aiming to develop more efficient LSTM variants that can maintain high performance while reducing model complexity. This paper introduces a novel architecture called CF-LSTM, which is based on the concept of CF networks and aims to streamline the CF-LSTM structure. CF-LSTM replaces portions of traditional LSTM cells with CF units and integrates them back into the existing LSTM framework. Experimental evaluations across multiple datasets demonstrate the superiority of CF-LSTM over the original LSTM and other approximate LSTM models. The results indicate significant reductions in parameters and memory usage, coupled with enhanced performance. Furthermore, this paper presents both qualitative and quantitative assessments of the model, highlighting its potential benefits and draw-backs in real-world applications.

Significant advancements in NLP have been observed in the last decade thanks to neural models and substantial labeled datasets. However, NLP models are often hindered by a reliance on extensive data availability, hindering their application to resource-constrained settings and unique tasks necessitating large-scale labeling. As a means of enhancing NLP data efficiency, data augmentation techniques have been investigated in recent years. A systematic examination of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings has been lacking until now, resulting in difficulty in comprehending the efficacy of diverse methods in various contexts. This study provides a comprehensive survey of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings, encompassing an overview of methods such as token-level and sentence-level augmentations, along with experiments conducted on 11 datasets across topics like classification, inference, and generation. Our research enables the formulation of recommendations to guide practitioners in selecting suitable augmentations tailored to different settings and highlights potential avenues for future investigation in NLP.

The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within conformal field theories (CFTs), especially those with an extensive state count, also known as "tower doubles." Under these conditions, the theory's extremal states are extremal CFTs (ECFTs), characterised by an extreme entropy density at high energies. It is conjectured that tower doubles universally exhibit the largest possible central charge values within their respective families. The central charge self-duality hypothesis holds the potential to locate the boundary of the convex convexity of charge spectra within CFTs.

To stabilize the estimation of ground and excited states on a quantum computer, we modify the quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) to utilize the model space. This model-space QITE method iteratively expands the model space while maintaining its orthogonality, enabling simultaneous description of multiple states. We enhance model-space QITE by integrating the quantum Lanczos algorithm, which boosts its convergence rate. In simulations, our approach outperforms both standard quantum Lanczos and the folded-spectrum QITE in calculating excited states. We show that spin contamination can be mitigated through an imaginary time propagator shift, efficiently obtaining excited states beyond the first. Additionally, we successfully compute low-lying electronic states of helium and water molecules in various configurations.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate the connection between the tight Hilbert function and its lower bound, achieving this condition implies that the ring is $F$-rational. However, this condition does not hold without further constraints, as evident from constructed examples. Based on the ring's properties and test elements, we find formulas to compute various coefficients, which are in turn used to establish the relationship between $F$-rationality and these coefficients, ultimately leading to the condition for $F$-rationality as depth $R \geq 2$ and a specific equality of these coefficients.

The rapid growth of renewable energy sources is altering grid stability, necessitating advanced control methods to prevent system overloads. The use of redispatch and coordination between distribution system operators has been shown to optimize use of distribution systems and minimize overscheduling risks. This study aims to encourage the active participation of large-scale generation assets in ancillary energy markets by analyzing their redispatch benefits. The proposed approach involves a non-cooperative game model incorporating accurate redispatch region calculations and realistic market revenue predictions. As the number of market players increases, the model converges to an efficient outcome. Furthermore, this work explores the impacts of bid strategy on social welfare and participant profits, revealing the potential drawbacks of utilizing high-order bids in market dispatch calculations.

R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the Galois theory of p-adic numbers and algebraic function fields over finite fields.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the $\sqrt{s}=13\,\textrm{TeV}$ LHC using the $\textrm{ATLAS}$ dataset, we have performed a detailed signal assessment. The analysis focuses particularly on distinguishing between the Higgs boson decaying into two bottom quarks and one such quark paired with a anti-quark in the channel where both Higgs bosons decay into top quark pair antipairs. To do this, we utilized an existing, well-established $\textrm{ATLAS}$ channel for single Higgs boson detection, which involves two legs in the final state consisting of top quark pair antipairs. Furthermore, we have explored the sensitivity of this channel to detect Higgs boson self-coupling deviations by simulating various scalar lambda c coefficients during the run period, specifically during the $\textrm{ATLAS}$ experiment's phases.

We calculate one-loop corrections to the Standard Model process of a Z boson emitting a Higgs boson, considering extended scalar sector scenarios for the Standard Model, including inert doublets and various triplets, quintuplets, and septuplets with different new scalar SU(2)L representations. These new scenarios are expected to be probed at a precision of a part in 10^4 by future e+e- colliders due to precise measurements of σ(e+e- → Zh) that complement searches for the Standard Model scalar sector at particle colliders such as the Large Hadron Collider, or a possible future pp collider, or Higgs decay to photons. We also find the sensitivity of σ(e+e- → Zh) and γγ decays of the Higgs boson to have the most notable complementary role in the complex triplet model scenario.

Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strengthening temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude and displayed a hexagonal shape. This indicates that a specific type of atmospheric wave, previously thought to force the distinctive hexagonal pattern, is prevalent in the stratosphere of Saturn.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period.

We present a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

The manner in which the surface of materials is terminated has significant implications for their physical characteristics, especially near critical transitions where the phase can shift abruptly, such as in the case of the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$. Researchers investigated the metal-insulator transition in thin V$_2$O$_3$ films and found that the way the surface is terminated has a profound effect on the transition's nature and that this influence eventually diminishes as the thickness of the film increases. A notable temperature-dependent discontinuity was found at the center of the insulating phase's valley, which likely signifies a transition between two distinct states within the same insulator phase, with the difference ultimately determined by the way the surface is terminated. Furthermore, a theoretical model incorporating an improper polarization was able to capture the observed features of the phase diagram and the structure of the insulating phase's valley.

Our study uncovers new features of non-equilibrium behavior in quantum double dark-soliton states for one-dimensional repulsive boson gases. We find a specific scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states that can be used to analyze quasi-condensation in weakly coupled quantum double dark-soliton states. We first demonstrate the precise time-dependent density profile of a quantum double dark-soliton state via the Bethe ansatz method. Next, we derive an effective macroscopic wave function for these states by calculating the amplitude and phase of field operator matrix elements. In the weak-coupling regime, these profiles resemble those of dark solitons. We then precisely calculate the quasi-condensation fraction in quantum double dark-soliton states and reveal that their non-equilibrium dynamics are governed by the competition between quasi-condensation and dark-soliton like behavior. Finally, we apply a quasi-condensate/dark-soliton effective model to describe the dynamics of quantum double dark-soliton states.

We create a linearisation functor for full linearisation that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. Our analysis defines the image of the full linearisation functor, resulting in a subcategory within the category of k-fold vector bundles. This subcategory features morphisms consisting of k+1 bodies and (k-1)-fold Elvers connections. We establish an equivalence between objects in this subcategory and certain geometric configurations known as k-kernels.

This informal note begins by illustrating some technical concepts, including the re-normalization of measures on orbital integrals from the works of Langlands, Frenkel-Langlands-Ng\^o, and Altug's research on Beyond Endoscopy. We discuss specific measures related to algebraic tori and explain how they relate to Tamagawa numbers. We then examine the GL2 case in depth. Additionally, the appendix by Matthew Koster clarifies the connection between the geometric measure of orbits and Kirillov's measure of co-adjoint orbits within the dual space of certain Lie algebras, including sl2 and so3.

The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature that could lead to a new method of x-ray imaging using synchronized, intense, bright light sources. An initial demonstration of 1D phase retrieval is conducted using photon scattering off electric fields, with a precise amplitude and phase reconstruction achieved from the data, validating the accuracy of the proposed phase retrieval algorithm.

By linking quantum error correcting codes to models of disordered classical statistical mechanics and examining the phase diagram of these models, researchers have found a valuable tool for studying how these codes resist errors under various noise conditions. This study expands this mapping to account for realistic faulty quantum circuits when describing quantum error correcting codes. First, based on a detailed circuit noise model, we develop a strongly correlated classical spin model corresponding to each circuit noise scenario. This approach is illustrated using the quantum repetition code, where we simulate the impact of periodically malfunctioning stabilizer readout circuits. We utilize Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the phase diagram resulting from these interactions, and our findings are compared with the performance of a minimum-weight perfect matching decoder. This research provides a method for assessing the fundamental error thresholds of quantum error correcting codes, independently of any specific decoding strategies, and could help inform the design of near-term quantum computing hardware.

Recent theoretical predictions suggest that certain group VI elemental monolayers, such as sulfur, selenium, and tellurium, may possess hidden topological insulator properties when placed on a substrate. This feature becomes non-local when these monolayers are exposed to oxygen. To investigate this, a range of oxidation configurations for the S monolayer have been studied, along with other group VI elements, using first-principles computations. Various oxidation derivatives exhibited significant, robust second-order topological insulator behavior. This was verified with electronic density analyses and by modeling the response to polarization fields. Notably, in the case of tellurium oxide, this behavior could only be sustained when oxidation was confined to the center of the lattice. This study reveals that oxidized elemental monolayers could potentially serve as sensitive indicators for detecting and localizing strain in their lattice.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybridizing techniques in conjunction with a new post-processing technique to effectively address the varied permeability characteristics. This approach leads to the development of a robust numerical scheme that results in a robust and stable method for solving this complex problem, as long as the blocking fractures do not intersect or form closed loops within the mesh elements. Our approach is validated through a variety of numerical experiments.

A comprehensive examination of a spin-triplet superconducting device, which involves a spiral magnetic arrangement, is presented. The underlying substrate exhibits an non-uniform magnetization ordered at a nanoscale, altering the parallel alignment required by superconducting pairs. This phenomenon has a significant impact on the length at which the pairs maintain their coherence. The interplay between the substrate's effects and the effects of the surrounding environment is analyzed, revealing that the substrate can actually increase the pairs' coherence length. The theoretical findings are validated through a case study of La$_{2/3}$Ba$_{1/3}$MnO$_3$.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors are commonly employed to compare alternative hypotheses and even theory-laden elements such as cognitive theories and instrument calibrations. However, many studies focusing on Bayes factors utilize simplified examples that do not reflect the complex theoretical comparisons typically made. We aim to fill this gap by demonstrating how Bayes factors can be calculated for non-obvious theoretical comparisons using real data and without making restrictive assumptions. Specifically, we use reaction time and accuracy data related to visual salience processing and the endogenous allocation of attention, relating these findings to attentional filtering theory.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets like Glue and SuperGLUE. Additionally, this research examines the connection between discourse indicators and sentence representations from the perspective of linguistic pragmatics.

We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under high-temperature and vacuum conditions.  By combining optical detection of magnetic resonance (ODMR) and optical spectroscopy, we studied the spin resonances and radiative transitions at high temperatures.  Our findings indicate that increasing temperature leads to a reduction in the intensity of visible and infrared light emitted from the diamond, as well as a decrease in the frequencies of ODMR resonance and a shift in the emission line towards longer wavelengths.  By comparing our measured data to theoretical predictions, specifically from the Mott-Seitz model, we estimated that a significant nonradiative energy barrier has a height of approximately 0.23 electron volts.

The backpropagation algorithm, though effective for training neural networks, has a significant drawback: it mandates the sharing of weights. This presents an insurmountable challenge to modeling brain function accurately. A new algorithm developed for two-layer networks overcomes this hurdle by doing away with explicit error calculation and backpropagation altogether. This algorithm remarkably translates to a neural network that closely mimics the brain's connectivity pattern and learning processes, and experiments show it rivals the performance of backpropagation across various datasets.

Using a bond-operator transformation, we derive a fundamental description in terms of spin-bosons for a $SU(3)$ variant of the anti-ferromagnetic Heisenberg spin model on a triangular lattice in large-$p$ limit, and then we analyze its low-energy behavior by employing a Schwinger-boson approach. For this basic model, we establish a $SU(2)$ symmetric effective theory on a half-filled Fermi surface, and we demonstrate that strong correlations give rise to emergent interactions among the fermions. Perturbing this scenario, we calculate the leading order contributions to these correlations, and our findings suggest that the system may exhibit a metallic, possibly topological, state for certain parameter ranges, at least in smaller systems. Our initial results for non-interacting fermions, and those obtained through numerical simulations and exact diagonalizations, are presented for comparison.

A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently compute accurate HF results for a large system evaluating the ground states of an electron gas in a harmonic confinement. The method implements a full HF method, self-consistently incorporating both direct and exchange correlation integrals. The method is versatile and can be applied to various confined electronic systems, including metallic traps and highly charged ions. The method uses time propagation to determine the lowest-energy solutions via the conditionally stable time propagation (CSTP) algorithm. The method efficiently evaluates exchange integrals and requires minimal storage for direct integrals. To test the method, three cases were evaluated: a two-dimensional electron gas in a harmonic trap, a three-dimensional electron gas in a harmonic potential, and a three-dimensional metallic trap. The method demonstrated the capability to evaluate HF ground states for these systems.

The capability of complex systems to maintain specific states and improve performance across various applications including speech recognition and grid stability. However, the underlying mechanisms that explain and predict these functional states remain unclear, hindering further development. Research on criticality in complex systems with built-in stability reveals multiple coexisting states and spontaneous state changes. In this context, we illustrate and investigate the ordered and disordered states of self-propelled particles within viscosity-like interaction networks. Our research shows that these systems exhibit stability-like phases and exhibit coexistence between ordered and disordered states. Moreover, we identify a critical network structure that separates these states and results in the formation of dynamic clusters at its threshold.

We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits three distinct regions: a global minimum area, an intermediate region containing stationary and non-convex subregions, and a highly curved non-convex region near the boundary of the feasible range. We demonstrate that applying Nesterov's heavy ball gradient descent with an appropriately tuned parameter can avoid the problematic higher curvature region and converge to a desired solution, while analyzing the geometry of the Burer-Monteiro landscape under the given Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time. We apply this research to matrix completion and show that a specific factorization approach with global potential for matrix completion can be solved efficiently to achieve convergence.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in another graph that mimics a specific power of the original graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, aiming to determine the exact or upper bounds of the chromatic number for specific types of graphs like path powers and cycle powers. In 2017, a significant advancement was made byhzr who calculated the exact values of the chromatic numbers for specific cycle power graphs C^k_7 and K_n, while also proposing new upper bounds for other related graphs K_n^2, W_n^2, and T_n^2.

Let $q\ge 3$ be an integer, with $\chi$ denoting a Dirichlet character modulo $q$ and $L(s,\chi)$ being the associated Dirichlet L-functions. This paper will present specific function series, along with novel identities linking the L-functions with Gauss sums, particularly focusing on identities related to $L(2,\chi)$.

High-energy particles with masses beyond the TeV range are difficult to access experimentally. Current constraints from Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis already set a strict limit on their lifespan, at under 0.1 seconds. Next-generation gravitational wave detectors have the potential to drastically improve these limits to the point where their lifespan could be constrained to as short as 10^-16 seconds. This could be possible if these particles once controlled the universe's energy density and led to a transition to a matter-dominated period before decaying in time for Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis to occur. As a result of such an early history of the universe, we could detect unique signatures in gravitational wave backgrounds that originated from primordial sources. Furthermore, we propose that detecting the gravitational wave spectrum from long-lived objects like cosmic strings can serve as a probe of fundamental particle physics parameters, ultimately providing more stringent constraints on the universe's early conditions through various UV extensions of the Standard Model. This has already led to constraints on the mass and coupling constants of hypothetical heavy particles and could be as low as several hundred MeV.

Our experiments examine how the geometric structure of force-free rigid swimmers interacts with different fluid properties, specifically focus on linear viscoelastic fluids of the Maxwell type. By using a generalized Bell-shaped swimmer that can adapt to various forms, we find that certain viscoelastic properties combined with certain geometries can cause the swimmer to move 4.5 times faster than in a Newtonian fluid. These optimal configurations result in significant elastic recoil flow but minimal overall overall flow. Furthermore, we discover that a Newtonian resistance law common among small swimmers may actually lead to increased swimming speed in viscoelastic fluids, while also identifying that highly viscoelastic fluids can make swimming harder for Bell-shaped swimmers.

We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms to develop strategies for a stochastic game, aiming to investigate the impact of social-learning algorithms on convergence to equilibrium. Our study involved testing algorithms on an information game, which has multiple Nash Equilibria and serves as a benchmark for counterfactual regret minimization. Our results showed that algorithms incorporating previous game history successfully converged to specific Nash Equilibria, whereas algorithms relying solely on past game outcomes failed to achieve equilibrium convergence. Additionally, we found that collaborative algorithms outperformed individual learners in terms of final payoff, verified equilibrium convergence through analysis of previous game histories, and identified potential applications in areas like automated trading.

The growing threat landscape in cybersecurity demands increased vigilance, 
wherein existing vulnerability information can be utilized to enhance knowledge 
and predictive analytics for risk mitigation. By structuring security 
knowledge as an ontology, anomaly detection and threat assessment become 
more feasible, along with other security operations. Nevertheless, 
traditional methods of enriching ontologies based on natural language 
processing and machine learning are hampered by issues in extracting contextual 
conceptual relationships from text. Therefore, sequential Deep Learning 
models, capable of handling the inherent sequences in language, are proposed 
for security-conceptual extraction from text, following a multi-step process 
that includes embedding, sequential feature learning, concept classification, 
and security-relational detection. The experimental results confirm the 
efficacy of this approach in security-conceptual extraction, outperforming 
existing methods in precision.

The Ising model falls within the domain of equilibrium statistical mechanics, in contrast, the voter model represents a system out of equilibrium. Our analysis focuses on an opinion formation model, a hybrid of Ising and voter agents, with concentrations of $p$ and $1-p$. Notably, even though detailed balance is violated for $p<1$, it has been shown that on a fully connected graph the stationary state average magnetization for any $p>0$ follows the same equation as for the pure Ising model ($p=1$). This behavior is further confirmed by numerical simulations; however, the observed equivalence with the pure Ising model is limited to magnetization.
